	<item>
		<title>Ad Attacking Cooper Makes False Connection to Murder</title>
		<link>https://www.factcheck.org/2026/08/ad-attacking-cooper-makes-false-connection-to-murder/</link>
		
		<dc:creator>Robert Farley</dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 26 Aug 2026 19:47:41 +0000</pubDate>
				<category>FactCheck Posts</category>
		<category>2026 Ads</category>
		<category>2026 elections</category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://www.factcheck.org/?p=285762</guid>

					<description><p><img width="640" height="273" src="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/Roy-Cooper-720-x-307.png" class="attachment-medium_large size-medium_large wp-post-image" alt="" style="float:left; margin:0 15px 15px 0;" decoding="async" fetchpriority="high" srcset="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/Roy-Cooper-720-x-307.png 720w, https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/Roy-Cooper-720-x-307-340x145.png 340w" sizes="(max-width: 640px) 100vw, 640px" />An ad from a super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley features a heart-wrenching testimonial from the father of a woman who was murdered in 2025. The ad falsely implies the accused murderer was one of the prisoners released during the COVID-19 pandemic when Whatley's Democratic opponent, Roy Cooper, was governor of North Carolina. Cooper had nothing to do with the accused murderer's release.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://www.factcheck.org/2026/08/ad-attacking-cooper-makes-false-connection-to-murder/">Ad Attacking Cooper Makes False Connection to Murder</a> appeared first on <a href="https://www.factcheck.org">FactCheck.org</a>.</p>
</description>
										<ns3:encoded><img width="640" height="273" src="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/Roy-Cooper-720-x-307.png" class="attachment-medium_large size-medium_large wp-post-image" alt="" style="float:left; margin:0 15px 15px 0;" decoding="async" srcset="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/Roy-Cooper-720-x-307.png 720w, https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/Roy-Cooper-720-x-307-340x145.png 340w" sizes="(max-width: 640px) 100vw, 640px" />
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">An ad from a super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley features a heart-wrenching testimonial from the father of a woman who was murdered in 2025. The ad falsely implies the accused murderer was one of the prisoners released during the COVID-19 pandemic when Whatley&#8217;s Democratic opponent, Roy Cooper, was governor of North Carolina.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The problem: Cooper had nothing to do with the accused murderer&#8217;s release. The suspect was released from a prison in South Carolina, not North Carolina.</p>


<div class="wp-block-image">
<figure class="alignleft size-full"><img decoding="async" width="243" height="219" src="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/MW-BUG-2026.png" alt="" class="wp-image-281925" srcset="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/MW-BUG-2026.png 243w, https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/MW-BUG-2026-161x145.png 161w" sizes="(max-width: 243px) 100vw, 243px" /></figure>
</div>


<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Here&#8217;s how the ad from the <a href="https://www.factcheck.org/2026/08/senate-leadership-fund-5/">Senate Leadership Fund</a>, or SLF PAC, tiptoes the line, implying, but not directly stating, that Cooper was indirectly responsible for the woman&#8217;s death.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">&#8220;Logan was the most caring, loving person,&#8221; Stephen Federico, the father of a 22-year-old murdered in 2025, says in the ad while choking back tears. &#8220;It was a home invasion. Went to the house where Logan was sleeping and he pulled her out of bed and forced her on her knees and stuck a shotgun in her, left side of her chest, and pulled the trigger for no reason. Logan was a casualty of an agenda. Roy Cooper let 3,500 criminals out on the street; 18 of them were murders. Forty years of Roy Cooper is enough.&#8221;</p>



<div style='position:relative;width:100%;padding-top:56.25%;padding-bottom:40px;'><iframe loading='lazy' style='position:absolute;top:0;right:0;left:0;bottom:0;width:100%;height:100%;' src='https://platform.adimpact.com/viewer/f730fc6c-5db8-44ef-88ea-88a244690213' frameborder='0' scrolling='no' allowfullscreen=''></iframe></div>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The claim about Cooper releasing &#8220;3,500 criminals out on the street&#8221; refers to a court settlement reached during the COVID-19 pandemic. But there&#8217;s some important context missing from that narrative. As governor, Cooper resisted calls to release prisoners to ease safety concerns. He was sued by the American Civil Liberties Union and other activists. After a judge issued a preliminary injunction in favor of the ACLU and called on the state to come up with a plan to reduce the prison population, Cooper reached a settlement to allow the release of 3,500 prisoners. But again, none of them was the man accused of killing Logan Federico.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">South Carolina did not expedite the release of prisoners during the pandemic (though it, too, was <a href="https://www.aclusc.org/news/were-suing-release-incarcerated-people-most-vulnerable-covid-19/">sued</a> by the ACLU and others). However, in addition to North Carolina, <a href="https://www.prisonpolicy.org/blog/2022/10/13/covid_policies/">numerous</a> other <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Prison_inmate_release_responses_in_response_to_the_coronavirus_(COVID-19)_pandemic,_2020">states</a> did implement expedited release policies to reduce their prison populations in response to the pandemic, including states like Iowa and Arkansas with Republican governors. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">We reached out to SLF PAC about its ad, but we did not get a response.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">&#8220;These attacks are false – this heinous crime was committed in South Carolina by a South Carolina criminal, but a Republican super PAC is using this tragedy for political gain,&#8221; a spokesperson for Cooper&#8217;s Senate campaign told us.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Cooper and Whatley are vying for an open Senate seat being vacated by Republican Thom Tillis, who is retiring. The Cook Political Report&nbsp;<a href="https://www.cookpolitical.com/senate/race/488626">says&nbsp;</a>that this Republican seat is the one Democrats &#8220;are most likely to flip.&#8221;</p>



<h2 class="wp-block-heading has-text-align-center">Logan Federico&#8217;s Murder</h2>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Logan Federico was a resident of North Carolina, but she was <a href="https://www.wcnc.com/article/news/crime/logan-federicomurder-stephen-federico-interview-death-penalty-repeat-offenders/275-ee23bd1f-e961-447e-953f-34532fdb9da2">visiting</a> friends in Columbia, South Carolina, when she was shot and killed in a home invasion. The man charged with killing her, <a href="https://columbiapd.net/2025/05/06/man-charged-in-fatal-cypress-street-shooting/">Alexander Dickey</a>, had a lengthy criminal history in South Carolina.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">A <a href="https://www.scribd.com/document/872357434/Newer-updated-SLED-Catch-file#from_embed">criminal history report</a> obtained by WIS News 10 in Columbia shows that prior to Federico&#8217;s murder, Dickey had been arrested nearly a dozen times and charged with nearly 40 crimes, including burglary and robbery. A WIS 10 <a href="https://www.wistv.com/2025/06/05/flaws-system-could-fixing-errors-have-saved-logan-federicos-life/">investigation</a> in June 2025 revealed that flaws in the criminal reporting system potentially contributed to a shorter sentence in 2023, on a charge that could have kept Dickey behind bars for years.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">As the WIS 10 investigation showed, Dickey was arrested in 2023 on a burglary charge and pleaded guilty to a first offense, third-degree burglary. But it wasn&#8217;t a first offense for third-degree burglary &#8212; Dickey had been sentenced for a first offense in 2014.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Rick Hubbard, the state&#8217;s 11th Circuit solicitor, told WIS 10 that his office did not know at the time about Dickey&#8217;s previous burglary arrests and convictions. So while Dickey could have <a href="https://scdailygazette.com/2025/10/02/father-of-slain-22-year-old-wants-federal-prosecutors-to-handle-daughters-murder-case/">faced</a> up to 10 years in prison, he was offered a plea deal for time served (411 days awaiting trial), and was placed on probation.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division, or SLED, said it never received fingerprints from the 2014 burglary arrest, so&nbsp;Dickey&#8217;s&nbsp;earlier conviction was not apparent to prosecutors.&nbsp;According to <a href="https://www.wistv.com/2025/06/05/flaws-system-could-fixing-errors-have-saved-logan-federicos-life/">WIS 10</a>, &#8220;Had they known, Hubbard said his office would not have prosecuted Dickey’s case as a first offense and Dickey would have likely received a longer sentence.&#8221;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Since his daughter&#8217;s murder, Stephen Federico has been a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F_qO5DzXsbU">prominent advocate</a> pushing lawmakers to keep repeat offenders behind bars for longer. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In April, South Carolina Republicans Sen. Lindsey Graham, who has since passed away, and Rep. Russell Fry <a href="http://web.archive.org/web/20260512032917/https://www.lgraham.senate.gov/public/index.cfm/press-releases?ID=83EB6F04-779D-48FC-8356-4E8642569D78">introduced</a> what was called <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/4462/titles">Logan&#8217;s Law</a>. The legislation, which has not made it out of committee, would create a publicly accessible violent criminal offender database (which is meant to hold judges and prosecutors accountable for lenient sentences), and would direct the creation of a report to Congress &#8220;identifying deficiencies in the sharing of fingerprint, warrant, and criminal history data between states and the federal government.&#8221;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">So, there appear to have been flaws in South Carolina&#8217;s criminal record-keeping on Dickey that may have kept him from being behind bars when he is alleged to have killed Federico. But none of that has anything to do with North Carolina, or Cooper.</p>



<h2 class="wp-block-heading has-text-align-center">Pandemic Prisoner Releases</h2>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In the ad, Stephen Federico says his daughter was &#8220;a casualty of an agenda.&#8221; He then immediately says, &#8220;Roy Cooper let 3,500 criminals out on the street; 18 of them were murders.&#8221;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Whatley, himself, has <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FNUIdI6oD9c">also</a> <a href="https://x.com/WhatleyNC/status/1990562420855877639">made</a> the prisoner release a key campaign issue.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">There were thousands of prisoners released early during the pandemic, but there&#8217;s important context missing from that attack. Cooper resisted early calls in the pandemic to commute sentences to reduce the prison population. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">On April 20, 2020, the ACLU, the NAACP and several inmates <a href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1o4B0dT2lDreGlxD9l3j52alG0WhBTAV7/view">sued</a> Cooper and other state prison officials saying they had &#8220;failed to meaningfully decrease the number of people in Department of Public Safety&#8221; facilities and that &#8220;[w]ithout timely relief from the courts, COVID-19 will continue to sweep through the state prisons, inflicting terrible suffering and death.”</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">On June 16 of that year, Wake County Superior Court Judge Vinston Rozier Jr. <a href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1SxQ2SpbqpsTuAVzSi0LIgY8xM0hE2iFc/view?usp=sharing">granted</a> a preliminary injunction to the plaintiffs, saying they were &#8220;likely&#8221; to &#8220;succeed on the merits of their claim that the conditions of confinement&#8221; violated the <a href="https://www.ncleg.gov/Laws/Constitution/Article1">state constitution&#8217;s</a> prohibitions against inflicting &#8220;cruel or unusual punishments.&#8221; The judge ordered the state to come up with a plan that would, in addition to other COVID-19 safety measures, reduce prison overcrowding.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Later, in December 2020, as COVID-19 cases in North Carolina prisons were rising, Rozier <a href="https://www.acluofnorthcarolina.org/press-releases/nc-court-appoints-special-master-oversee-protections-people-incarcerated-during/">appointed</a> a special master to review the state’s home confinement program and to provide recommendations for easing prison populations through eligible early release.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In February 2021, the two sides reached <a href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PuwiUaQqc0N9fz0D6SJ5Gcfo9bINMWhH/view">a settlement</a>, with the state agreeing to the “early reentry” of 3,500 people in state custody within six months. (The plaintiffs had <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20200415165942/http://www.thecharlottepost.com/news/2020/04/07/local-state/nc-gov.-cooper-urged-to-reduce-inmate-ranks-as-covid-19-defense/">sought</a> the release of as many as 18,000 prisoners.) According to <a href="https://www.theassemblync.com/news/politics/justice/roy-cooper-michael-whatley-prisoner-release-settlement-pandemic/">The Assembly</a>, a longform journalism news site, by the time the agreement was signed, more than 9,500 inmates had tested positive for COVID-19 and 47 had died.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">&#8220;After [Cooper] fought against these releases in court, North Carolina law enforcement officials and parole officers looked to similar criteria President Trump used a year prior when his administration released thousands of federal prisoners due to COVID-19,&#8221; a spokesperson for the Cooper campaign told us. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">As part of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act (the CARES Act) signed by Trump in late March 2020, more than <a href="https://www.bop.gov/inmates/fsa/docs/first-step-act-annual-report-june-2024.pdf">13,000 federal prisoners</a> were released from prison into home confinement. But the CARES Act <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/04/04/2023-07063/office-of-the-attorney-general-home-confinement-under-the-coronavirus-aid-relief-and-economic">excluded</a> any prisoners convicted of violent crimes, sex offenses and terrorism-related crimes. That wasn&#8217;t entirely the case in North Carolina. While state officials initially indicated only nonviolent offenders would be among those released early, prison officials later <a href="https://www.wral.com/archive/19553809/">clarified</a> that some violent offenders due to be released in 2021, the year of the settlement, would also be included (provided they had served their minimum sentence).</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The Charlotte Observer <a href="https://www.charlotteobserver.com/news/politics-government/article314664852.html">reported</a> that the list also included 51 inmates serving life sentences. State officials say all were eligible for parole before the deal, and were not made eligible because of it. (In any case, the Cooper campaign says law enforcement officials and parole officers made the determinations about which prisoners were released, not Cooper.)</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The agreement was criticized at the time by some Republicans, who argued Cooper should have continued to fight in court. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“A group I consider more liberal than me has sued an administration I consider more liberal than me, and a deal was reached,” Republican state Rep. Carson Smith <a href="https://carolinapublicpress.org/43232/prison-settlement-a-balancing-act-between-political-risk-and-public-health/">said</a> a week after the agreement was announced.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Representatives of the plaintiffs, however, described Cooper as consistently adversarial.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“The idea that, you know, Roy Cooper is somehow being attacked for doing too much here [to suport prisoner releases] is the most absurd thing I’ve ever heard,” Daniel Bowes, director of policy and advocacy at the ACLU of North Carolina, <a href="https://carolinapublicpress.org/43232/prison-settlement-a-balancing-act-between-political-risk-and-public-health/">told</a> Carolina Public Press in March of 2021.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">As the pandemic unfolded, &#8220;what we saw was a constant sort of reluctance to provide meaningful release,&#8221; Bowes said. &#8220;There was absolutely no sort of urgency that wasn’t pushed along by the litigation.”&nbsp; </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“It was an extremely adversarial litigation,&#8221; Emancipate NC attorney Elizabeth Simpson <a href="https://www.theassemblync.com/news/politics/justice/roy-cooper-michael-whatley-prisoner-release-settlement-pandemic/">told</a> The Assembly.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Orlando Rodriguez, special deputy attorney in the North Carolina Department of Justice, who represented the defendants, told Carolina Public Press the state feared more orders from the judge were coming. Indeed, the special master appointed to the case &#8220;said he was going to recommend that the state broaden the categories for who would be eligible for release,&#8221; Carolina Public Press reported.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The SLF ad also says that of the 3,500 prisoners released &#8220;18 of them were murders.&#8221;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">That&#8217;s based on an analysis published in the <a href="https://nypost.com/2026/05/07/us-news/nearly-half-of-inmates-released-under-nc-gov-roy-cooper-during-covid-have-reoffended-including-18-charged-with-murder/">New York Post</a> on May 7 &#8212; and cited in the ad &#8212; that concluded nearly half of the 3,500 prisoners released went on to commit another criminal offense, many of them violent offenses.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">While the ad leaves the impression that 18 of the people released were murderers, it&#8217;s actually that &#8212; as the New York Post put it &#8212; &#8220;A staggering 18 of the prisoners released have been charged with murder in the four years since.&#8221;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">An <a href="https://www.theassemblync.com/news/politics/justice/roy-cooper-michael-whatley-prisoner-release-settlement-pandemic/">analysis</a> by The Assembly, however, concluded the New York Post story was misleading.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">&#8220;Our analysis found that of the roughly 3,000 inmates who were released early because of the settlement, more than 90% would have been out by the end of 2021 anyway by virtue of completing their sentences,&#8221; The Assembly story stated. &#8220;The agreement allowed prison officials to let them out early through a variety of methods—awarding credits for things like good behavior to shave time off their sentences, releasing qualified nonviolent inmates to house arrest, and accelerating parole for eligible inmates serving life or long active sentences under a previous sentencing structure.&#8221;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Indeed, the Cooper campaign pointed out that more than half of the 18 individuals cited in the Post as murderers are alleged to have committed that crime after their scheduled pre-settlement release date for previous convictions. According to <a href="https://www.theassemblync.com/news/politics/justice/roy-cooper-michael-whatley-prisoner-release-settlement-pandemic/">The Assembly</a>, &#8220;at least seven of them were already out of prison before the settlement was even signed.&#8221; In other words, the Cooper campaign argues, the settlement had no part in most of the murders identified by the New York Post. &nbsp;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Whatley campaign spokesman DJ Griffin said, &#8220;While Cooper had the opportunity to fight this settlement in court (like Democrat Governors in Colorado and Illinois), he chose to settle, releasing thousands of convicted criminals back onto our streets.&#8221; Griffin claimed a number of people have been murdered&nbsp; by &#8220;criminals Roy Cooper released from prison early.&#8221;&nbsp;</p>

		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://www.factcheck.org/?p=285746</guid>

					<description><p><img width="640" height="273" src="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/nrsc-ad.png" class="attachment-medium_large size-medium_large wp-post-image" alt="" style="float:left; margin:0 15px 15px 0;" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/nrsc-ad.png 720w, https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/nrsc-ad-340x145.png 340w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 640px) 100vw, 640px" />In the Ohio Senate race, a Republican ad blames former Sen. Sherrod Brown for a deadly crash in April on an Ohio interstate in which an immigrant was charged with vehicular homicide. But there’s no evidence of any tie between Brown's votes on immigration, as the ad suggests, and the suspect in this incident.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://www.factcheck.org/2026/08/the-nrscs-weak-ties-between-brown-and-deadly-interstate-crash-in-ohio/">The NRSC&#8217;s Weak Ties Between Brown and Deadly Interstate Crash in Ohio</a> appeared first on <a href="https://www.factcheck.org">FactCheck.org</a>.</p>
</description>
										<ns3:encoded><img width="640" height="273" src="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/nrsc-ad.png" class="attachment-medium_large size-medium_large wp-post-image" alt="" style="float:left; margin:0 15px 15px 0;" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/nrsc-ad.png 720w, https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/nrsc-ad-340x145.png 340w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 640px) 100vw, 640px" />
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In the Ohio Senate race, a Republican ad blames former Sen. Sherrod Brown for a deadly crash in April on an Ohio interstate in which an immigrant was charged with vehicular homicide. But there’s no evidence of any tie between Brown&#8217;s votes on immigration, as the ad suggests, and the suspect in this incident.</p>


<div class="wp-block-image">
<figure class="alignleft size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="243" height="219" src="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/MW-BUG-2026.png" alt="" class="wp-image-281925" srcset="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/MW-BUG-2026.png 243w, https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/MW-BUG-2026-161x145.png 161w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 243px) 100vw, 243px" /></figure>
</div>


<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“Because of him, Ohioans paid the price,” <a href="https://host2.adimpact.com/admo/viewer/30ded2e3-63e7-4c57-9aee-628d176f4853">the ad</a>, from the National Republican Senatorial Committee, claims, referring to <a href="https://www.congress.gov/member/sherrod-brown/B000944">Brown</a>, who was elected to the U.S. House in 1993 and then served in the Senate from 2007 to 2025. Brown is challenging Republican Sen. Jon Husted in the toss-up race.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">We’ve <a href="https://www.factcheck.org/2014/09/the-rest-of-alaskas-crime-story/">seen</a> campaign ads <a href="https://www.factcheck.org/2014/10/a-willie-horton-ad-in-nebraska/">in the past</a> trying to tie a deadly incident to the policies of a politician. But the links can be tenuous, at best, as is the case here. Most of the votes the NRSC cites didn&#8217;t make a difference in terms of whether legislation was ultimately enacted, and it&#8217;s hard to know how the bills would&#8217;ve affected this particular case.<br><br>The NRSC ad began airing this month, mostly through streaming TVs or devices, according to the ad-tracking service AdImpact. The spot begins by saying, “Sherrod Brown opened our borders to dangerous illegals,” and then shows an image of a border wall along with images of Brown and former President Joe Biden as the announcer says, “The consequences were deadly.”</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">That leaves the impression that something Biden and Brown did allowed a dangerous person to enter the country. But the case the ad goes on to discuss involves an immigrant who entered the country sometime in the 1990s, according to the Ohio Department of Public Safety, and it’s unclear how or where he came into the country. The man – Modou Ngom – later used different names to obtain a driver’s license and then citizenship, the Ohio DPS said.</p>



<div style='position:relative;width:100%;padding-top:56.25%;padding-bottom:40px;'><iframe loading='lazy' style='position:absolute;top:0;right:0;left:0;bottom:0;width:100%;height:100%;' src='https://platform.adimpact.com/viewer/30ded2e3-63e7-4c57-9aee-628d176f4853' frameborder='0' scrolling='no' allowfullscreen=''></iframe></div>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">An investigation by Ohio authorities found that it &#8220;appears&#8221; Ngom &#8220;used multiple names and dates of birth to obtain state and federal identification,&#8221; according to an April 23 statement by the director of the Ohio DPS. Ngom got his Ohio driver&#8217;s license around 2003, his commercial driver&#8217;s license in 2007, &#8220;under an alternate identity,&#8221; and his citizenship in the mid-2010s, &#8220;under that same alternate identity,&#8221; the statement said. &#8220;State records show he changed his name back to Modou Ngom in 2015.&#8221;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The Ohio DPS said it gave its information about Ngom to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno, a Republican, sent <a href="https://www.moreno.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/moreno-demands-investigation-denaturalization-after-illegal-immigrant-trucker-kills-3-in-ohio/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">an April 28 letter</a> to the secretaries of the departments of Transportation and Homeland Security, asking them to investigate. Moreno posed several questions, including, &#8220;When, through what port of entry, and under what justification did Ngom enter the United States?&#8221; and &#8220;Did Ngom use fraudulent immigration documents in the process of obtaining state and federal identification?&#8221; We reached out to DHS to ask if it could provide any additional information about Ngom, but we haven&#8217;t yet received a response. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The NRSC ad shows a snippet of a TV news broadcast about the <a href="https://fox8.com/news/fiery-fatal-crash-in-delaware-county-involving-nine-vehicles-closed-i-71-for-hours/">April 11 deadly crash</a> in Delaware County, Ohio, for which Ngom <a href="https://www.10tv.com/article/news/local/columbus-semi-driver-deadly-interstate-71-crash-delaware-county-fraud-investigation-ohio-dps/530-ca03514c-a19a-4bd4-a085-d9ad4c759c8d?tbref=hp">has been charged</a> with multiple counts of aggravated vehicular homicide and vehicular assault. The semi-truck he was driving hit a car from behind, leading to a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wHolJWer17I&amp;t=35s">multi-car crash</a>, with some vehicles catching on fire. A family of three <a href="https://www.cleveland.com/nation/2026/04/ohio-couple-1-year-old-child-killed-in-multi-vehicle-crash.html">was killed</a>: &#8220;37-year-old Luke Soposki, 36-year-old Lynnea Soposki, and their 1-year-old child,&#8221; as the news clip in the ad says.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The ad pins the blame for the tragedy squarely on Brown, ending with the line, “Because of him, Ohioans paid the price.”</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">What does the former senator have to do with it? An NRSC spokesperson told us the Republican committee was tying Brown to Ngom through Brown&#8217;s votes on immigration legislation, claiming Brown voted for &#8220;open border policies&#8221; and &#8220;to protect illegal aliens like Ngom from deportation.&#8221;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">For any legislation to have had an impact on Ngom entering the country, it would&#8217;ve had to be enacted before he reportedly came to the U.S. sometime in the 1990s. The NRSC cites one vote by Brown in the 1990s <a href="https://clerk.house.gov/Votes/1996432">against a 1996 immigration bill</a> &#8212; <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/104th-congress/house-bill/2202">legislation</a> that then President Bill Clinton <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/104th-congress/house-bill/3610/text">signed into law</a> a few days later. The legislation &#8212; which aimed to crack down on illegal immigration by, among other measures, increasing the number of Border Patrol agents, constructing border fencing and expediting deportations &#8212; <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1996/09/29/us/house-backs-deal-on-budget-for-97-in-bipartisan-vote.html?searchResultPosition=3">was rolled into</a> an omnibus appropriations bill that Brown <a href="https://clerk.house.gov/Votes/1996455">voted</a> in favor of.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">So, Brown&#8217;s initial vote against the immigration bill made no difference in terms of what became law. It&#8217;s also difficult to say how passing or not passing the legislation would&#8217;ve had an impact on Ngom, given we have scant details about him and his immigration to the U.S.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Many Democrats opposed the 1996 immigration bill and proposed their own version, which Brown <a href="https://clerk.house.gov/Votes/1996431">supported</a> and which failed. News coverage at the time said that some of the opposition from Democrats and initially the White House concerned provisions regarding legal immigrants, including one that would have blocked medical care for legal immigrants who had AIDS and another &#8220;that would have barred legal immigrants who were poor enough to qualify for food stamps from acting as sponsors to other newcomers,&#8221; a Sept. 29, 1996, New York Times article <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1996/09/29/us/house-backs-deal-on-budget-for-97-in-bipartisan-vote.html?searchResultPosition=3">said</a>. Republicans agreed to drop those elements from the final appropriations bill.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The NRSC points to other votes by Brown as detailed in a May <a href="https://www.foxnews.com/politics/dem-senate-candidate-sherrod-brown-claims-supports-closing-border-gop-says-record-proves-otherwise">Fox News article</a>. But several of those votes also didn&#8217;t matter in the end in terms of what was enacted into law, or not. For instance, Brown co-sponsored a <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/senate-bill/1591/all-info">2019 bill</a> to repeal a <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2017/01/30/2017-02102/enhancing-public-safety-in-the-interior-of-the-united-states">2017 executive order</a> by President Donald Trump to prioritize removing immigrants in the country illegally who had been charged with or convicted of crimes, or committed fraud, and to withhold federal grants from so-called &#8220;sanctuary&#8221; jurisdictions if local officials don’t cooperate with federal immigration officials. The bill died, never getting a vote in Congress.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Another item cited in the Fox News article is Brown&#8217;s vote against a 2021 <a href="https://www.congress.gov/amendment/117th-congress/senate-amendment/3742/all-info">amendment</a> to a <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/senate-concurrent-resolution/14">congressional budget resolution</a>. A budget resolution doesn&#8217;t become law, but <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48284">serves as a guide</a> for the fiscal year budget and spending and revenue levels for a period of time. The amendment <a href="https://www.congress.gov/amendment/117th-congress/senate-amendment/3742/text">said</a> Congress could revise allocations to make sure ICE has resources &#8220;to detain and deport a higher number of illegal aliens who have been convicted of a criminal offense&#8221; as long as the changes didn&#8217;t increase the deficit. But the amendment passed anyway, and it&#8217;s unclear if it would even pertain to Ngom, who at that point reportedly was a citizen. It&#8217;s also not clear if he had been convicted of any crimes.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In a 2001 vote listed in the Fox News article cited by the NRSC, Brown <a href="https://clerk.house.gov/Votes/2001242" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">supported</a> an amendment that failed. The Democratic sponsor of the amendment <a href="https://www.congress.gov/amendment/107th-congress/house-amendment/186/text">described</a> it as ensuring &#8220;due process&#8221; for some immigrants, per a Supreme Court ruling at the time. The measure sought to halt the deportation of immigrants under certain legal conditions, such as for those with plea agreements in place before the 1996 immigration law took effect or for those without final orders of removal. But, again, the amendment failed. <br><br>Other votes highlighted in the Fox News article concern Brown&#8217;s opposition to Trump&#8217;s border wall. But of course those came long after Ngom reportedly entered the country and even after Ngom reportedly obtained citizenship.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The NRSC certainly disagrees with Brown&#8217;s votes and his positions on immigration, and that&#8217;s a matter of opinion. We take no position on that. But none of the votes it cites indicates a connection to Ngom, as its ad contends.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">When we asked the Brown campaign about the ad, it responded that the former senator had worked &#8220;to secure the southern border,&#8221; pointing to his yes vote for a <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/senate-bill/4361">2024 border security bill</a> that was endorsed by the labor union for Border Patrol agents. The president of that group <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/new-immigration-bill-senate-bipartisan-border-patrol-endorsement-rcna137354">described</a> the bill as &#8220;not perfect&#8221; but &#8220;a step in the right direction.&#8221; The bill failed. Brown also <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/senate-bill/1600">co-sponsored</a> a 2023 Democratic border security appropriations bill, which also failed to advance. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The campaign further cited Brown being an original co-sponsor of the bipartisan <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/senate-bill/1271/cosponsors">FEND Off Fentanyl Act</a>, which <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/house-bill/815/text">became law</a> in 2024 and sought to stem fentanyl trafficking by cartels, among other measures. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The Brown campaign pointed to the candidate&#8217;s <a href="http://youtube.com/watch?v=AY-Q6Anmq5w&amp;t=378s">recent remarks</a> on immigration to a Youngstown, Ohio, TV news station in April. &#8220;I support closing the border to people that, so they just can&#8217;t cross the border at will,&#8221; Brown said, prompting criticism from Republicans of his legislative history as detailed in the May Fox News article. &#8220;We of course should be deporting people that have committed a crime,&#8221; Brown continued. &#8220;But we&#8217;ve also seen these mass arrests and deportations that are disrupting families who are here working every day paying taxes, paying into Social Security, paying into Medicare. Those are the kinds of people that I want to see in this country who are doing the work they ought to do.&#8221;</p>

If you prefer to give by check, send to: FactCheck.org, Annenberg Public Policy Center, P.O. Box 58100, Philadelphia, PA 19102. </em></p>

		<item>
		<title>Trump’s ‘No Tax on Tips’ Claim Doesn’t Add Up</title>
		<link>https://www.factcheck.org/2026/08/trumps-no-tax-on-tips-claim-doesnt-add-up/</link>
		
		<dc:creator>Angela Lin</dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 25 Aug 2026 17:55:58 +0000</pubDate>
				<category>FactCheck Posts</category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://www.factcheck.org/?p=285432</guid>

					<description><p><img width="640" height="273" src="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/trump_no_taxes_tips2.jpg" class="attachment-medium_large size-medium_large wp-post-image" alt="" style="float:left; margin:0 15px 15px 0;" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/trump_no_taxes_tips2.jpg 720w, https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/trump_no_taxes_tips2-340x145.jpg 340w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 640px) 100vw, 640px" />The White House has provided no federal data to support President Donald Trump's claims that because of his "no tax on tips" policy, “440,000 tipped workers” in Nevada “saved an average of $10,000 on their taxes,” and “130,000 tipped workers” in Georgia “saved an average of more than $7,000 on their taxes.”</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://www.factcheck.org/2026/08/trumps-no-tax-on-tips-claim-doesnt-add-up/">Trump&#8217;s &#8216;No Tax on Tips&#8217; Claim Doesn&#8217;t Add Up</a> appeared first on <a href="https://www.factcheck.org">FactCheck.org</a>.</p>
</description>
										<ns3:encoded><img width="640" height="273" src="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/trump_no_taxes_tips2.jpg" class="attachment-medium_large size-medium_large wp-post-image" alt="" style="float:left; margin:0 15px 15px 0;" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/trump_no_taxes_tips2.jpg 720w, https://cdn.factcheck.org/UploadedFiles/trump_no_taxes_tips2-340x145.jpg 340w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 640px) 100vw, 640px" />
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The White House has provided no federal data to support President Donald Trump&#8217;s claims that because of his &#8220;no tax on tips&#8221; policy, “440,000 tipped workers” in Nevada “saved an average of $10,000 on their taxes,” and “130,000 tipped workers” in Georgia “saved an average of more than $7,000 on their taxes.”</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Instead of actual tax savings, the president may have been referring to the average amount some workers in those states were able to deduct from their federal taxable income in 2025. The actual savings would be a fraction of that, depending on a person&#8217;s tax rate.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The president also may be exaggerating the number of Nevadans and Georgians who were able to claim a tips deduction.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Trump talked about the savings for tipped workers in Nevada during an economic speech at the Red Rock Casino Resort and Spa in Las Vegas on Aug. 5.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">&#8220;This past filing season, 440,000 tipped workers right here in Nevada saved an average of $10,000 on their taxes,&#8221; he <a href="https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-economy-taxes-las-vegas-august-5-2026/">said</a>. &#8220;Think of that, just on the no tax on tips. So, that means every worker saved — this is put out by the government, check it out. … They say, ‘Oh, it wasn’t $10,000. It was $9,912.’ Think of it, every worker made $10,000 more money. That’s all because of the fact that I said I was going to do it and I got it done.”</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">He made a similar <a href="https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-high-school-marietta-georgia-july-22-2026/">claim</a> in a July 22 speech in Georgia, in which he said, “This past filing season, 130,000 tipped workers right here in Georgia saved an average of more than $7,000 on their taxes. And that&#8217;s because of no tax on tips.”</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">When we asked for supporting evidence, White House spokesman Kush Desai said that the administration’s tax policies were helping Americans nationwide save money – but he did not provide the “government” source for Trump’s figures.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“President Trump is right: tens of millions of working-class Americans are saving thousands of dollars on his signature no tax on tips, overtime, and Social Security provisions in the Working Families Tax Cut. That is especially true in Nevada, the birthplace of President Trump’s no-tax-on-tips pledge,” Desai said in an emailed statement.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">However, we did not find support for the president’s claims.</p>



<h2 class="wp-block-heading has-text-align-center">A Deduction Isn&#8217;t the Amount Saved in Taxes</h2>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">On July 4, 2025, Trump signed into law the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which, among other things, <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/1/text">created</a> a temporary federal income tax deduction of up to $25,000 in qualified tips. The deduction – which is available each tax year from 2025 through 2028 – begins to <a href="https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/what-the-no-tax-on-tips-deduction-means-for-you">phase out</a> when modified adjusted gross income exceeds $150,000 for a single filer or $300,000 for a married couple filing jointly. The deduction is <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/13/2026-07104/occupations-that-customarily-and-regularly-received-tips-definition-of-qualified-tips">reduced</a> by $100 for every $1,000 above those thresholds.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">So, although Trump refers to this tax policy as “no tax on tips,” the law does not eliminate all taxes on tipped income. Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/13/2026-07104/occupations-that-customarily-and-regularly-received-tips-definition-of-qualified-tips">still apply</a>, for example.&nbsp;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">More important, a federal tax deduction does not reduce taxes paid dollar for dollar. It reduces the amount of income on which the IRS calculates federal income tax, as <a href="https://taxpolicycenter.org/author/aparna-mathur">Aparna Mathur</a>, a senior fellow at the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center, explained to us in an email.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“What the President is referring to is not the actual tax savings from the tips deduction, but likely the average amount of income that a tipped worker is deducting from their taxable income,” Mathur wrote. “This is not a direct reduction in taxes but rather a reduction in income subject to taxes.”</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">For example, based on the <a href="https://www.irs.gov/filing/federal-income-tax-rates-and-brackets">federal tax brackets</a> for 2025, if a tipped worker with taxable income between $11,926 and $48,475, with a 12% marginal tax rate, received a $10,000 deduction from their federal taxable income, the tax savings from that deduction would be about $1,200. If that same person received a $7,000 deduction, their federal income taxes would be reduced by $840.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In theory, as the deduction amount and marginal tax rate increase, so does the potential tax cut. As the Bipartisan Policy Center <a href="https://bipartisanpolicy.org/explainer/whats-driving-higher-tax-refunds-in-2026/">noted in February</a>, the largest tax cut possible would be about $6,000 for someone in the 24% tax bracket with the highest gross income – $150,000 for a single filer and $300,000 for a married couple – allowed to claim the full $25,000 tip deduction.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">But Mathur said the tax savings would be lower for people who already have little income tax liability due to claiming the standard federal tax deduction, which <a href="https://apps.irs.gov/app/vita/content/00/00_13_005.jsp">in 2025</a> was $15,750 for individual filers and $31,500 for married couples. “If their taxable income is already close to zero, there is no further tax liability to reduce, so the tips deduction provides them no additional value,” she said.&nbsp;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Meanwhile, the <a href="https://taxpolicycenter.org/taxvox/budget-laws-tax-cuts-overtime-and-tips-are-popular-few-will-benefit">Tax Policy Center</a> estimated in August 2025 that about 3% of U.S. households would benefit from the deduction of tipped income, and it estimated an average savings of about $1,400 among those households. Trump’s own White House Council of Economic Advisers had <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/09/22/2025-18278/occupations-that-customarily-and-regularly-received-tips-definition-of-qualified-tips">estimated</a> in June 2025 that the tax provision for tipped income would increase affected workers’ average take-home pay by about $1,300 a year.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“It’s hard to think of a realistic scenario where the average tipped worker gets a tax savings equal to $7000 or $9000,” Mathur said. But she told us that the Tax Policy Center has not produced state-level estimates.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Notably, in a June 2 <a href="https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0517">press release</a>, the Treasury Department said that through the April tax-filing deadline, more than 7.5 million tax filers in the U.S. had used the tips deduction, and the department reported an “average deduction of over $7,000.”</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The White House <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/04/in-nevada-president-trump-celebrates-no-tax-on-tips-real-money-to-working-americans/">used</a> similar language in an April news release in which it said 6 million tax filers nationwide had reported an average tips deduction exceeding $7,100 at that point in the filing season.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The Treasury and White House releases did not refer to the $7,000 figure as a tax cut, refund or the average amount saved by taxpayers.</p>



<h2 class="wp-block-heading has-text-align-center">Number of Beneficiaries Unknown</h2>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">It&#8217;s also unlikely that 440,000 tipped workers in Nevada and 130,000 in Georgia claimed the tips deduction, as Trump said.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In a September 2025 <a href="https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/no-tax-on-tips-covers-more-than-440000-nevadans-heres-why-few-will-actually-benefit">analysis</a>, the Nevada Independent, an online news outlet, reported that “approximately 444,000 Nevadans, or more than a quarter of the state’s workforce, could theoretically be covered by the No Tax on Tips provision of the Republican megabill.” But it said, “the number who will actually see more money in their pockets is likely far lower.&#8221;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The Nevada Independent calculated that large figure by taking a preliminary Treasury Department list of tipped professions affected by the tax policy and cross-referencing it with Bureau of Labor Statistics data on the estimated number of people in Nevada working in those occupations.&nbsp;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">But Yale Budget Lab Associate Director of Policy Research John Ricco <a href="https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/no-tax-on-tips-covers-more-than-440000-nevadans-heres-why-few-will-actually-benefit">told</a> the news outlet that the Treasury&#8217;s list was overly broad. &#8220;Not everyone who works in these occupations will get tips,&#8221; Ricco was quoted as saying.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In 2024, the Tax Policy Center <a href="https://taxpolicycenter.org/taxvox/tipped-workers-their-income-taxes-and-states#:~:text=Tipped%20workers%20make%20up%20different,the%20workforce%20in%20Southern%20states.">estimated</a> that the number of tipped employees in Nevada was much lower – about 5% of its workers, or <a href="https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/LASST320000000000005">about 80,000</a> people as of June.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Then in April, when the Treasury and the IRS finalized <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/13/2026-07104/occupations-that-customarily-and-regularly-received-tips-definition-of-qualified-tips">federal regulations</a> defining qualified tips and listing the jobs “that customarily and regularly received tips” on or before Dec. 31, 2024, they noted that broad federal occupation codes sometimes combine tipped and non-tipped jobs. They also warned against using the provided occupation codes as the sole measure of whether workers customarily received tips. Tax-return <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/13/2026-07104/occupations-that-customarily-and-regularly-received-tips-definition-of-qualified-tips">data</a> included in the regulation show why.&nbsp;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In the 2023 tax year, 82.8% of people in the relevant bartender category reported at least $100 in tips, according to a table that was included in the published regulations. The figure was 74.5% for wait staff and 70.9% for gambling dealers. The percentages fell sharply in other eligible professions. Only 11% of dishwashers, 2.7% of maids and housekeeping cleaners, and 0.1% of electricians reported at least $100 in tips, the data show.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">So, counting every worker in those occupation groups would likely produce a much larger figure than the actual number of people who reported qualified tips.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">It’s less clear where Trump may have gotten the figure of 130,000 Georgia workers claiming the tips deduction.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The Georgia Department of Labor <a href="https://dol.georgia.gov/press-releases/2026-08-20/georgia-sets-new-records-labor-force-and-employment-july">reported</a> 5.3 million employed state residents as of July. Trump’s 130,000 figure would be about 2.5% of that number.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In its <a href="https://taxpolicycenter.org/taxvox/tipped-workers-their-income-taxes-and-states#:~:text=Tipped%20workers%20make%20up%20different,the%20workforce%20in%20Southern%20states.">2024 analysis</a>, the Tax Policy Center, citing the Yale Budget Lab, said that about 2% of workers nationally held jobs that regularly received tips. TPC found higher percentages in many Southern states.&nbsp;</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">That could support 130,000 as a rough estimate of Georgia workers in tipped occupations, but it still does not mean that 130,000 people in the state took the federal deduction and received tax savings as a result.&nbsp;</p>
